entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bozorgmehr, a legendary Persian polymath and vizier of the Sasanian Empire, flourished in the late 5th and early 6th centuries CE, serving notably under Shahanshah Kavadh I (r. 488–531 CE) and his son Khosrow I Anushirvan (r. 531–579 CE). Though his exact birth year is debated, tradition places his active period around 450-501 CE. He is celebrated as the epitome of Sasanian wisdom, statesmanship, and intellectual prowess, embodying the sophisticated cultural synthesis characteristic of the classical Persian empire before the advent of Islam. His reputation as a sagacious advisor and scholar ensured his enduring significance in Persian history and literature, often associated with the golden age of Sasanian intellectual life centered in Ctesiphon.

Bozorgmehr's most significant contributions lie in the realm of cultural transmission and intellectual development. He is widely credited with translating the Indian collection of fables, the *Panchatantra*, from Sanskrit into Middle Persian (Pahlavi) under the title *Karīrag ud Damanag*, which later became the foundational *Kalila wa Dimna* in Arabic, profoundly influencing global literature. Furthermore, he is traditionally believed to have introduced the game of chess to the Sasanian court from India, transforming it into a popular pastime and metaphor for strategic thinking. Several Pahlavi texts, such as the *Andarz-i Wehzad Farrokh-Pirooz* (Book of Counsel of Bozorgmehr), are attributed to him, showcasing his philosophical and ethical insights into governance and human conduct.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bozorgmehr's translation of the *Panchatantra* profoundly impacted global literature through the *Kalila wa Dimna*, while his legendary wisdom shaped ideals of statesmanship in Persian and Islamic cultures. His actions exemplify the Sasanian Empire's role as a vital nexus of cultural exchange between East and West.
